messages.body_plain:
Hi.

On Thu, Oct 30, 2008 at 2:25 PM, haile...@gmail.com
<haile...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Hi,
>
> Because I want to get the copy number of all samples with all snp id,
> so I followed the "calculating raw total copy number manully" steps.
> my question: 1 Did I do the right steps?

It looks correct to me.

>                    2If I analyzed the unpaired snp with different
> normal and tumor samples, I still want to get the similay reault.  Can
> I follwing the same steps ? But how to calculate the log2 ratio.

I'm not sure what your question/problem is: The log2 CN ratio for a
specific locus is defined as:

 M = log2(theta_i/theta_R)

where 'theta_i' refers to the theta for sample i and 'theta_R' to the
theta for the reference sample (R).  In an paired analysis, you pick
theta_R to be the value for the normal sample.  In a non-paired
analysis you have to decide what to use for theta_R, but typically it
is a robust average of the pool of available samples.   Some people
just want to use normals for this, some want to use both tumor and
normals.  In either case, if your set of reference samples is in
AffymetrixCelSet 'cesRef' then you calculate the reference signals as:

  ceRef <- getAverage(cesRef);

This reference can then be treated as if it was a hybridized sample
(indeed aroma.affymetrix don't "know" the difference).  FYI, you can
also extract the complete JxI theta matrix from 'cesRef' and do
rowMedians() on that to achieve the same, but be more memory efficient
and the result is persistent over time (it will not have to be
recalculated when you restart R).

Hope this helps

Henrik

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

you want to make the bottom margin larger, e.g.
par(mar=c(8,4,4,2)+0.1);  See graphical parameter 'mar' in help(par)
for more details.

/Henrik

Hi,

messages.body_plain:
Dear all:

First off, like many others already I would like to thank you for
aroma.affymetrix.

I'm just starting to learn how to use the software, and I've gotten
through the full CN analysis of 96 Affymetrix 6.0 chips (which took a
while!). The software works wonderfully and I have my results.

My question:  I have *very* noisy data (and this is not aroma's
fault!). The noise comes from extra amplification steps. The scale of
the noise is impressive, but there still is an average copy number
result, somewhere around 0.3 that seems to be consistent in some
chips. In others, the CN data is fragmented (many different CNs abound
on every chromosome) which looks like it's an effect of the noise.

Therefore, I'd like to increase a smoothing window in the process. I
apologize if this is already mentioned somewhere; can you point me if
possible to a way to increase the smoothing window? I'm not interested
in small CNs -- I'd be happy with large averaged regions as I'm
interested in aneuploidy on a chromosomal scale.

Thank you!

messages.body_plain:
Hi.

On Mon, Nov 3, 2008 at 10:05 AM, Deanne Taylor <theo...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Dear all:
>
> First off, like many others already I would like to thank you for
> aroma.affymetrix.
>
> I'm just starting to learn how to use the software, and I've gotten
> through the full CN analysis of 96 Affymetrix 6.0 chips (which took a
> while!). The software works wonderfully and I have my results.
>
> My question:  I have *very* noisy data (and this is not aroma's
> fault!). The noise comes from extra amplification steps. The scale of
> the noise is impressive, but there still is an average copy number
> result, somewhere around 0.3 that seems to be consistent in some
> chips. In others, the CN data is fragmented (many different CNs abound
> on every chromosome) which looks like it's an effect of the noise.
>
>
> Therefore, I'd like to increase a smoothing window in the process. I
> apologize if this is already mentioned somewhere; can you point me if
> possible to a way to increase the smoothing window? I'm not interested
> in small CNs -- I'd be happy with large averaged regions as I'm
> interested in aneuploidy on a chromosomal scale.

I don't think you want to smooth data before passing it on to a
segmentation method, but rather you want the segmentation method to
deal with the noise.  For both the CbsModel and the GladModel
segmentation classes, you, via fit(), can pass additional arguments to
the internal segmentation functions, that is, to segment() of DNAcopy
and glad() of GLAD, respectively.  See help for those function in the
corresponding package.

I second guess you that you are using the CbsModel for segmentation,
correct?  (please provide complete script next time).  I haven't
played with the tuning parameters for segment(), but you can tell to
post-prune identified regions by:

cbs <- CbsModel(cesN);
fit(cbs, arrays=1:3, chromosomes=4:6, undo.splits="prune");

There are several tuning arguments, so you'll have to try different
settings.  I hope you find a setup that works for you. For more help
on those, please ask the authors of the segmentation package you use.

Also, I tried, and you can even pass these parameters via the
process() of ChromosomeExplorer, e.g.

ce <- ChromosomeExplorer(cbs);
process(ce, arrays=1:3, chromosomes=4:6, undo.splits="prune");

Note, in both cases, if you want to refit already fitted
segmentations, you can do that by adding argument 'force=TRUE'.  An
alternative, at least when you play with different settings and want
to keep everything, you can add your own custom tags to the CbsModel
output, e.g.

cbs <- CbsModel(cesN, tags="*,prune");
fit(cbs, arrays=1:3, chromosomes=4:6, undo.splits="prune");

cbs <- CbsModel(cesN, tags="*,prune=0.10");
fit(cbs, arrays=1:3, chromosomes=4:6, undo.splits="prune", undo.prune=0.10);

etc.  Please feel free to share what you learn on this mailing list.
If you find something useful, we can add a paragraph on this to one of
the vignettes.  If you're really serious about it, we can add a
complete vignette illustrate what different settings does to the
segmentation.

Hope this helps

Henrik

> Thank you!

messages.subject_clean: [aroma.affymetrix] How to use FIRMA
messages.body_plain:
Hi.

Indeed, the manual is a bit sparse on this.  But, you are almost there.

------------
------------ from the web page
------------
Alternative Splicing Analysis (FIRMA)

The FIRMA analysis ONLY works from the PLM based on transcripts.

firma <- FirmaModel(plmTr)
fit(firma, verbose=verbose)
fs <- getFirmaScores(firma)

You can extract the firma scores in the same way as the transcript/
exon estimates with extractDataFrame() or readUnits() applied to fs.
------------
------------
------------

This last comment suggests you can use 'extractDataFrame' or
'readUnits' to get the FIRMA scores into some kind of tabular format
(Note that this may be a very big table or a very big list of tables
for extractDataFrame and readUnits, respectively).  For example, for
the first 10 units, you could do:

 > exFirma <- extractDataFrame(fs,addNames=TRUE,units=1:10)
 > exFirma[,6:ncol(exFirma)]<-log2(exFirma[,6:ncol(exFirma)])

For example:

 > exFirma[1:5,1:7]
   unitName groupName unit group cell huex_wta_breast_A
huex_wta_breast_B
1  2315251   2315252    1     1    1        0.15717297       -0.22563046
2  2315251   2315253    1     2    2       -0.06614846        0.23234612
3  2315373   2315374    2     1    3        0.61863822        0.06033641
4  2315373   2315375    2     2    4       -0.66929193       -0.50362466
5  2315373   2315376    2     3    5        0.64692440        0.08086550

Here, you can read off the FIRMA scores and the transcript [unitName]
and exon (PSR) [groupName] identifiers.

Cheers,
Mark

messages.subject: Re: [aroma.affymetrix] Re: Window smoothing and noisy CN data
messages.subject_clean: [aroma.affymetrix] Re: Window smoothing and noisy CN data
messages.body_plain:
Hi.

On Tue, Nov 4, 2008 at 7:02 AM, Deanne Taylor <theo...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> For the record, to process the 96 Affy 6.0 chips, I exactly followed
> the Total Copy Number Analysis (5.0 & 6.0) vignette. It was very
> helpful and everything worked perfectly.
>
> http://groups.google.com/group/aroma-affymetrix/web/total-copy-number-analysis-6-0
>
> I followed the vignette exactly, for the non-paired CNR case (common
> reference as robust average across samples).
>
> On my Macbook Pro, the TCNA of the 96 Affy 6.0 chips was going to take
> about a week to process the data (or so the output was telling me), so
> I switched over to a newer Windows server and it only took a day or so
> of aggregate time. The install and processing on the Windows server
> was seamless.

There can be many things causing your notebook to be so much slower.
Have a look at Page 'Improving processing time':

  http://groups.google.com/group/aroma-affymetrix/web/improving-processing-time

/Henrik

>
> Deanne
>
>
> On Nov 3, 10:57 pm, "Henrik Bengtsson" <h...@stat.berkeley.edu> wrote:
>> Hi.
>>
>>
>>
>> On Mon, Nov 3, 2008 at 10:05 AM, Deanne Taylor <theori...@gmail.com> wrote:
>>
>> > Dear all:
>>
>> > First off, like many others already I would like to thank you for
>> > aroma.affymetrix.
>>
>> > I'm just starting to learn how to use the software, and I've gotten
>> > through the full CN analysis of 96 Affymetrix 6.0 chips (which took a
>> > while!). The software works wonderfully and I have my results.
>>
>> > My question:  I have *very* noisy data (and this is not aroma's
>> > fault!). The noise comes from extra amplification steps. The scale of
>> > the noise is impressive, but there still is an average copy number
>> > result, somewhere around 0.3 that seems to be consistent in some
>> > chips. In others, the CN data is fragmented (many different CNs abound
>> > on every chromosome) which looks like it's an effect of the noise.
>>
>> > Therefore, I'd like to increase a smoothing window in the process. I
>> > apologize if this is already mentioned somewhere; can you point me if
>> > possible to a way to increase the smoothing window? I'm not interested
>> > in small CNs -- I'd be happy with large averaged regions as I'm
>> > interested in aneuploidy on a chromosomal scale.
>>
>> I don't think you want to smooth data before passing it on to a
>> segmentation method, but rather you want the segmentation method to
>> deal with the noise.  For both the CbsModel and the GladModel
>> segmentation classes, you, via fit(), can pass additional arguments to
>> the internal segmentation functions, that is, to segment() of DNAcopy
>> and glad() of GLAD, respectively.  See help for those function in the
>> corresponding package.
>>
>> I second guess you that you are using the CbsModel for segmentation,
>> correct?  (please provide complete script next time).  I haven't
>> played with the tuning parameters for segment(), but you can tell to
>> post-prune identified regions by:
>>
>> cbs <- CbsModel(cesN);
>> fit(cbs, arrays=1:3, chromosomes=4:6, undo.splits="prune");
>>
>> There are several tuning arguments, so you'll have to try different
>> settings.  I hope you find a setup that works for you. For more help
>> on those, please ask the authors of the segmentation package you use.
>>
>> Also, I tried, and you can even pass these parameters via the
>> process() of ChromosomeExplorer, e.g.
>>
>> ce <- ChromosomeExplorer(cbs);
>> process(ce, arrays=1:3, chromosomes=4:6, undo.splits="prune");
>>
>> Note, in both cases, if you want to refit already fitted
>> segmentations, you can do that by adding argument 'force=TRUE'.  An
>> alternative, at least when you play with different settings and want
>> to keep everything, you can add your own custom tags to the CbsModel
>> output, e.g.
>>
>> cbs <- CbsModel(cesN, tags="*,prune");
>> fit(cbs, arrays=1:3, chromosomes=4:6, undo.splits="prune");
>>
>> cbs <- CbsModel(cesN, tags="*,prune=0.10");
>> fit(cbs, arrays=1:3, chromosomes=4:6, undo.splits="prune", undo.prune=0.10);
>>
>> etc.  Please feel free to share what you learn on this mailing list.
>> If you find something useful, we can add a paragraph on this to one of
>> the vignettes.  If you're really serious about it, we can add a
>> complete vignette illustrate what different settings does to the
>> segmentation.
>>
>> Hope this helps
>>
>> Henrik
>>
>>
>>
>> > Thank you!
> >
>

messages.subject: How to improve processing time
messages.subject_clean: How to improve processing time
messages.body_plain:
Hi, I've created a new page called 'Improving processing time':

 http://groups.google.com/group/aroma-affymetrix/web/improving-processing-time

It show some tricks you can use to speed up the processing and things
to avoid which otherwise will kill your speed.

For users of Affymetrix most recent SNP & CN arrays (GenomeWideSNP_5 &
GenomeWideSNP_6), I've got good news.  In the most recent version of
the package, I've added a way such that the PLM can be fitted to all
single-probe CN units more or less instantaneously, which will speed
up the process if not 50% definitely substantially.  See above page
for more details.

Cheers

/Henrik

Hi,

it looks like you haven't *fitted* the PLM, because all chip effects
(theta:s) are reported to be zero on the intensity scale or -Inf on
the log-scale, cf.

> Total thetas:

> Summary of signals (on the log2 scale):
> Min. 1st Qu. Median Mean 3rd Qu. Max.
> -Inf -Inf -Inf -Inf -Inf -Inf

  Since the fragment-length effects are modeled on the log-scale,
there are no finite data points available for fitting the model, cf.

> Fitting target prediction function to each enzyme exclusively...
> Distribution of log2 signals that are finite:
> Mode FALSE NA's
> logical 233558 0

The package detects this an throws an exception and reports the problem, cf.

> [2008-11-06 10:12:41] Exception: Cannot fit target function to enzyme,
> because there are no (finite) data points that are unique to this enzyme: 1

Please please please, when you run into problems/get errors, always
provide us with your *complete* script and your sessionInfo().

Cheers

Henrik

messages.body_plain:
Hi.

On Thu, Nov 6, 2008 at 7:10 AM, EE_Aaron <adsk...@uh.edu> wrote:
>
> Hi,
>
> I would like to use methods AffymetrixCdfFile, AffymetrixCelSet to
> define data by passing as arg the full path and filename e.g. <.drive>
> \<path>\<filename> , where this may differ from the working directory.
> How might I do that?

The short (and very conservative) answer is: You don't want to do
this!  The package relies very much on a well defined directory
structure and you do not want to break this.  If you find yourself
specifying paths in any of your aroma.affymetrix scripts, that is a
very good indicator that you are doing something incorrect.

However, you can still preserve the correct directory structure and
have your files elsewhere.  You haven't told us your setup such as
operating system (please always as much information as possible to
help us help you, e.g. sessionInfo() is a minimum), so I cannot be
very specific, but see:

1) Section 'Using file links or Windows shortcuts' on Page 'Annotation Files':
http://groups.google.com/group/aroma-affymetrix/web/setup

2) My last reply on Oct 22, 2008 to Thread 'How do you analyze Gene ST Data?':
http://groups.google.com/group/aroma-affymetrix/browse_thread/thread/1db943fd36aec71a/

This should solve what you need (if not, let me know).

/Henrik

>
> Thanks,
> Aaron
>
> >

I don't know the specifics of Mac/OSX, but on Windows I've noticed
that R never returns any of the memory it allocates to the OS.  The
memory is only returned when the R process quits.  This is a problem
is the memory is fragmented and R needs to allocate a large chunk;
then the fragmented memory it has can't be used and additional memory
is requested from the OS.  I think this is the case on Windows, but
maybe/hopefully this is solved in OSX.   Thus, I occasionally restart
my R sessions to return memory.  You can safely do so as well, because
aroma.affymetrix will detect what is already processed and skip that.
That might help you with you immediate problem.

Check with 'top' to see how much memory the R session uses.  The 250K
arrays shouldn't consume too much memory and it should be rather
constant over time/number of arrays.  If it does, let me know.  There
might be some cached results in some of the objects that are not
cleaned output properly.

R is single-threaded so, unless you have compiled R specially, I think
it will only utilize one of your two cores.  Then the other processes
should be able to run on the free core.  Is that what your system
monitor reports too?

So, my best suggestion for now is to restart the R session.

/Henrik

messages.body_plain:
While R is single-threaded, on Mac OS X R links to Altivec which is a
multi-threaded BLAS. In order words: as soon as you do matrix algebra
you will utilize all of your cores. This is in general great, because
it speeds up the computations a lot (it is _really_ significant).
Unfortunately, it also implies that your computer can slow down if you
do big matrix computations. I do not know how to disable this, aside
from recompiling R (and an associated slowdown).

Kasper

Ok, I thought a bit more.

You can use "renice" on the command line to change the "nice" setting
of R, that should make your system way more responsive. There are a
few GUIs available, like Benicer, Renicer and Process Wizard (I have
not tried any of them).

Basically nice tells the system the priority of a program. Low values
is high priority, so if you change R to say 10 or higher it should
work. See also man nice and man renice

On the command line you can see the nice setting of the programs by
# ps xl
(lookf or column NI)

The only question is how this work when R calls Altivec, I am not an
expert on how nice is inherited.

Kasper

messages.subject: Re: Performance issue in Mac
messages.subject_clean: Performance issue in Mac
messages.body_plain:
I have no real performance issues running up to 70x250k arrays,
sometimes in 3 parallel analyses, on an 8 core Mac Pro (8GB RAM,
Leopard Server). Main bottleneck is HD read/write, which is alleviated
by using a RAID array (and having the system on a separate WD
Raptor ...).

But no general "system slowdown", as one gets sometimes while loading
Parallels etc.

Michael.

messages.body_plain:
Hi "sc@rcega",

I suspect that the fit(plm, verbose=TRUE) step was never
done/completed.  This was the cause of an almost identical problem
discussed last week, cf. Thread 'about: wrong information of CN 500k'
on Nov 6, 2008:

  http://groups.google.com/group/aroma-affymetrix/browse_thread/thread/6dfe3afc216f27fc/34442574ee1b039a

Note, it's helpful if you increase the verbosity of the output
message, i.e. use verbose=-20 or similar (verbose=TRUE corresponds to
verbose=-1).  That will give you more details on what is going on
before you get an error message, and you can do a better job on
troubleshoothing.

Hope this helps

Henrik

messages.subject: RE: GC correction for FFPE samples in SNP 6.0 arrays
messages.subject_clean: GC correction for FFPE samples in SNP 6.0 arrays
messages.body_plain:
Hi Henrik,

I've recently ran into the following article:

"Genome-Wide Copy Number Alterations Detection in Fresh Frozen and
Matched FFPE Samples Using SNP 6.0 Arrays"
GENES, CHROMOSOMES & CANCER 47:957–964 (2008)
Marianne Tuefferd,1*† An De Bondt,2† Ilse Van DenWyngaert,2 Willem
Talloen,2 Tobias Verbeke,3
Benilton Carvalho,...

It seems it provides the definitive evidence that the GC correction is
necessary for SNP 6.0 arrays, at least in case of FFPE samples.
I am wondering if you think it would be useful to add the GC
correction to aroma.affymetrix and if yes, could you provide some
guidelines on how to implement it?
Maybe you've  already done this or it's in your plan for the next version?.

Thank you,

Alex Lisovich

messages.body_plain:
Hi.

See comments below.

>
> qn <- QuantileNormalization(csBC, typesToUpdate="pm")
> csN <- process(qn, verbose=verbose)
>
> Then how to get the probeset data with labels(with probeset_id as row
> names, like a data frame)?

Just to clarify, do you want RMA summarization at the probeset level?
If so, you can use 'extractDataFrame' on a ChipEffectSet ... for
example:

plmEx <- ExonRmaPlm(csN, mergeGroups=FALSE)
fit(plmEx, verbose=verbose)
cesEx <- getChipEffectSet(plmEx)
ExFit <- extractDataFrame(cesEx, units=1:3, addNames=TRUE)

More details at:
http://groups.google.com/group/aroma-affymetrix/web/human-exon-array-analysis

> And for FIRMA,
>
> firma <- FirmaModel(plmEx)
> fit(firma, verbose=verbose)
> fs <- getFirmaScores(firma)
> exFirma <- extractDataFrame(fs,addNames=TRUE)
> exFirma[,6:ncol(exFirma)]<-log2(exFirma[,6:ncol(exFirma)])
> ....
>
> Suppose I have 100 samples which can be classified as 2 groups(50
> samples each group). After this step, how should I know which exon are
> differentially spliced in the two groups?

One way to do this would be to take the table of FIRMA scores (the
right most 100 columns of 'exFirma' above) and do a limma analysis (as
if you were looking for differential expression but operating directly
on the FIRMA scores).

Hope that helps.
Mark

messages.subject: Re: [aroma.affymetrix] RE: GC correction for FFPE samples in SNP 6.0 arrays
messages.subject_clean: [aroma.affymetrix] RE: GC correction for FFPE samples in SNP 6.0 arrays
messages.body_plain:
Hi Alex,

On Wed, Nov 12, 2008 at 4:19 PM, Alex Lisovich <alex.l...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Hi Henrik,
>
> I've recently ran into the following article:
>
> "Genome-Wide Copy Number Alterations Detection in Fresh Frozen and
> Matched FFPE Samples Using SNP 6.0 Arrays"
> GENES, CHROMOSOMES & CANCER 47:957–964 (2008)
> Marianne Tuefferd,1*† An De Bondt,2† Ilse Van DenWyngaert,2 Willem
> Talloen,2 Tobias Verbeke,3
> Benilton Carvalho,...
>
> It seems it provides the definitive evidence that the GC correction is
> necessary for SNP 6.0 arrays, at least in case of FFPE samples.
> I am wondering if you think it would be useful to add the GC
> correction to aroma.affymetrix and if yes, could you provide some
> guidelines on how to implement it?
> Maybe you've  already done this or it's in your plan for the next version?.

There is actually a GcContentNormalization class (that operates on
summarized data, i.e. ChipEffectSet:s).  This implements the
(optional) GC correct step in Section 3.2.5 of the CRMA paper:

H. Bengtsson; R. Irizarry; B. Carvalho; T. Speed, Estimation and
assessment of raw copy numbers at the single locus level,
Bioinformatics, 2008. [pmid: 18204055] [doi:
10.1093/bioinformatics/btn016]

Note that in that 500K study, with that set of data and set of
preprocessing methods, we saw no effect of doing (probe) GC-content
normalization.  I'm not saying it is useful to correct for, but I
should be careful saying that there "definitive evidence" that it is
needed.  I say this, because I see fragment-length normalization,
GC-content normalization, curve-fit ("loess") normalization and a few
other normalization methods as correcting for *symptoms* in data, but
not necessarily the *cause*.  If one can correct for the real cause,
many of these symptoms actually goes away.  One such cause is
non-linearity in data and especially offset.  One of the strengths
with allelic-crosstalk calibration (one implemented in CRMA) is
actually that it corrects for offset and by doing so downstream
symptoms goes away.  For instance, see Fig 2 in the CRMA paper showing
that it corrects for differences in empirical distributions, i.e.
although tempting to do quantile normalization, the real cause is
simply a single offset term.  Same reasoning does indeed apply to
fragment-length normalization and what I believe also GC-content
normalization.

Back to the GcContentNormalization method: Since we saw little need to
GC-content normalization, that class has been somewhat forgotten over
time and I haven't made sure that it works with the newer chip types.
It works only with 10K-500K arrays, iff one gets the correct
annotation data files from the CNAT program.  I'll have to update this
to work with these newer chip types.  However, in the meanwhile I
think a good proxy will be to use probe-position sequence
normalization, which is readily implemented for all Affymetrix chip
types.  This will be explained in the CRMA v2 vignette, which is on my
to do list.

So, stay tuned.  I'll post a message to the list when the CRMA v2
vignette is available.

/Henrik

>
> Thank you,
>
> Alex Lisovich
>
> >
>

If you do 'combineAlleles=FALSE' in the setup of the RmaCnPlm, you
will get allele-specific estimates.  You can then continue with
fragment-length normalization and segmentation as is.

Also, in this case extractTheta(cesN) will return (thetaA, thetaB)
estimates.  When you do combineAlleles=TRUE, you will get the total
theta estimates.

You should expect to get even better results when the CRMA v2
preprocessing method comes out, because it will control also for
allelic imbalances in addition to other things.

not using the lastest version of aroma.affymetrix, so please update

>
> 1) I'm doing CNV analysis for 8 patients comparing each one to the

> and I
> have to force quit then restart the whole analysis. This is taking

>

Yes, I think this the problems you are reporting (here and below) has
to with the generation of PNG files.  The fact that you have problem
with x0064 and x00128 images and big chromosomes, which generate very
wide PNG images, indicates that there is a memory issue.  This has
nothing to do with the package per se, but the PNG driver used.

In R, there are now several different graphical drivers that can be
used to generate PNGs and their performance and quality depends on the
operating system etc.  From the verbose output, it looks to me that in
your case you are using the Cairo PNG device driver of the Cairo
package (there is now also a default Cairo driver in R), but to be
sure, what does:

> print(findPngDevice())

report.  If you see something like:

function (...)
{
    Cairo::CairoPNG(..., bg = NA)
}
<environment: 0x032903e4>

then you use the Cairo driver in the Cairo package.  If so, then
thread 'ChromosomeExplorer memory leaks' (Aug 18, 2008) is useful; it
reports similar issues, identifies Cairo to be the cause, and suggests
two alternative PNG drivers: (i) the default png() of R and png2() or
R.utils.  The person in that thread had problems with the former, but
success with the latter.

To use the png2() driver (PNG via postscript and ghostscript), do:

findPngDevice <- function(transparent=TRUE, ...) {
  if (transparent) {
    function(...) { png2(..., type = "pngalpha"); par(bg=NA); }
  } else {
    function(...) png2(...);
  }
}

at the beginning of your script.

Let us know if this helps

Henrik

from your verbose output below I see that you are using the CbsModel
class for doing CN segmentation.  This class is using the (fast)
Circular Binary Segmentation (CBS) method implemented in the DNAcopy
package and described in detail in the two CBS papers:

[1] Olshen, A. B.; Venkatraman, E. S.; Lucito, R. & Wigler, M.
Circular binary segmentation for the analysis of array-based DNA copy
number data. Biostatistics, 2004, 5, 557-572
[2] Venkatraman, E. S. & Olshen, A. B. A faster circular binary
segmentation algorithm for the analysis of array CGH data.
Bioinformatics, 2007

The 2nd is an follow up paper/improvement and that is what's
implemented in DNAcopy.

For interpretation of these results, I recommend reading these papers
and emailing the authors.  The Bioconductor mailinglist is better
suited for discussing segmentation results in general.  Although very
interesting, I will have very little time participating in such
discussion (unless I start developing my own methods).

If you wonder about the graphic annotation, then the horizontal blue
dashed lines are the CN levels for CN=1, CN=2, CN=3 on the log2-scale.
 The cytoband on top is the same cytoband as generated by the 'GLAD'
(segmentation) package.  Lavina Gordon made some comments on these in
thread '

http://groups.google.com/group/aroma-affymetrix/browse_thread/thread/75d289f449643151/f5238e2ecc6eef2c?lnk=gst&q=lavinia+blue#f5238e2ecc6eef2c

contributions.  It can be spell/grammar corrections, single sentences

Hi Mohsen.

On 17/11/2008, at 11:37 PM, Mohsen Khorshid wrote:

> Hello Mark,
>
> Thank you indeed for spending time and replying my email.
>
> One question: do you really want to use the 'full' CDF?  It depends on
> your situation, but you have to realize what this imposes on the
> analysis.  In a lot of cases, the full CDF will include a lot of
> probesets that are essentially measuring nothing (at least in my
> experience, this is what I see).  I wouldn't use it as a first pass.
> Are you after specifically novel transcriptional units, or
> differential splicing of annotated genes?
>
> we are studying a potential splicing function on a few protein
> binding. To do that we have two control replicates  and 4 silenced
> treatments. The 4 are coming from 2 different siRNA (A,B) to
> minimize the off-targets effects of the siRNAs. In this case I
> decided to use full version not to miss anything.

Your call.  The core collection of probesets is pretty comprehensive
of the annotated genes.  I don't think 'full' really means not missing
anything.  I worry that having a bunch of probesets at background in
genes that exhibit differences in expression may just throw up high-in-
magnitude residuals that are not really of interest.  Do let the list
know how you go with it though.

> > I understand that the table is huge but I am giving R memory.limit
> of
> > 3600 MB and I am using a machine which have 4 GB of RAM on Windows
> > Vista 32bits so I wonder how can I extract this data?!
> > I even tried to write it in a file using write.table it didn't work
> > either. Is it because I have used the full version of the CDF file?
>
>
>
> When you say write.table "didn't work", what actually did not work?
>
> > Question2:
> > Is it possible to get help with a detialed R script in order to
> > generate the FIRMA scores represented by color scale for all
> probesets
> > corresponding to "differentially spliced exons/transcripts"? How
> can I
> > use Limma on that? - probably the same way that it have been
> presented
> > in FIRMA paper Purdom et al (June 2008).
>
> I'm not exactly sure what you are after here.  Are you looking for a
> way to plot the FIRMA scores for a single transcript?  If so, I have
> some code that might be useful to gather the information needed to use
> the 'GenomeGraphs' package.  What figure in the Purdom et al. paper
> are you referring to?  That would help us direct you.
>
> Well it would be good because I can perhaps check 20 targets that I
> "assume" are targeted by this RNA-binding protein using deep
> sequencing. Basically I was looking for generating the plots shown
> in supplementary documents(supplementary Data 2.pdf)
> http://bioinformatics.oxfordjournals.org/cgi/data/btn284/DC1/2
>
>
> Could I in any how ask you how to generate them?

Elizabeth has some code for this.  From what I last heard, she was
going to wait for a few bits of code to be incorporated into the
GenomeGraphs package before releasing it.  I'm not sure if she was
planning to make a fully generic function, there are generally many
customizations the user may want to do and its hard to cater to
everything.

It may be best to familiarize yourself with the GenomeGraphs package.
The vignette shows an example with exon array data.  Basically, the
supplementary figures are just a set of 'image' plots or 'matplot'
plots of the raw or processed data.

> And, I assume you are going to use limma on your matrix of FIRMA
> scores (N x 6 where N is the number of probesets) to identify
> probesets of interest.
>
> Exactly. Is it possible to ask on that?

Sure.

> I just wanted to know if I want to cite FIRMA I should put
> aroma.affymetrix included as well or the FIRMA paper.

Up to you.  I personally would probably cite both, aroma.affymetrix is
an integral part of the infrastructure that allows FIRMA to work.

Cheers,
Mark

Hi Mohsen.  More below.

On 19/11/2008, at 3:30 AM, Mohsen Khorshid wrote:

> Hello,
>
> Thank you very much for your answers.
>
> I have used the "core" version and it works thank you again. I could
> also save it in tab delimited file.
> Could you please explain these  columns of the FIRMA score table:
> unitName
> groupName
> unit
> group
> cell

units = genes or transcript clusters
group = probeset (as defined by Affymetrix)

unitName is the identifier (what the identifier is depends on what CDF
you used), unit is just an index.  groupName will by the Affymetrix-
defined probeset identifier, group is just an index.  For FIRMA
scores, cell should always be 1 (I think).

> Is the unit corresponding to probesets?! How can I extract the
> expression level of an exon.

unit != probeset, at least not what Affy calls a probeset.  Unit
corresponds to the collection of probesets for a transcript cluster.
Affy has probe selection regions (PSRs) which is roughly an exon, but
sometimes there are multiple probesets per exon.

You could get the probeset RMA summaries. From http://groups.google.com/group/aroma-affymetrix/web/human-exon-array-analysis
, it says:

-------------
...
There are two options, regardless of the kind of custom CDF you use.
To fit a summary of the entire transcript (i.e. estimate the overall
expression for the transcript), do:

plmTr <- ExonRmaPlm(csN, mergeGroups=TRUE)
print(plmTr)

Otherwise, to fit exon-by-exon, change the value of mergeGroups to
FALSE in the ExonRmaPlm() call above.

plmEx <- ExonRmaPlm(csN, mergeGroups=FALSE)
print(plmEx)
-------------

You can do the latter one and later on in that web page, it shows you
how to 'getChipEffectSet' and 'extractDataFrame' ...

> For example I would like to get the expression level of exon
> ENSE00000756202 in ENSG00000111780? How do you map the "unit ids" to
> "ensemble exon ids"?

This is tricky.  But, its really just a matter of matching genome
coordinates.  You'll need to know the coordinates of your ENSE, which
you can get from Biomart (or the biomaRt R package) and Affymetrix
gives you a file (CSV) of the coordinates of each probeset.

> About the visualization:
> I am sorry for confusion. I have been looking at GenomeGraphs about
> a week ago. This is mostly showing the exons of one transcript. What
> specifically I need is to generate the is to visualize the firma
> scores represented by colors in each CEL files for let's say 20
> transcripts.

OK, so you don't want plots like the supplementary data?  How about
just extracting the matrix of FIRMA scores for those 20 transcripts
and using the 'image' command?

Hope that helps.

Mark

>
> > Dear Henrik and Mark,
>
> > Thanks so much for your replies. I am going to work through your
> > responses and try again. I did get confused by the directory structure
> > and naming conventions. What I would like to do is have all of my
> > annotation files in one location (Network Drive W) as these are shared
> > by multiple folks in my group. The we I perform an experiment I would
> > like all analysis and output that is generated to be stored in the
> > appropriate directory on a different location (Network Drive X). As I
> > understand the aroma.affymetrix directory requirements, everything
> > must be in the rawData and the annotationData directories, both of
> > which must be in the same path. Is that correct?
>
> Yes, it is correct that aroma.affymetrix needs to see annotationData/
> and rawData/ in the current working directory.   This is on purpose
> and design to make life easier (indeed).  This way we do not have to
> specify paths in our scripts, because aroma.affymetrix knows where to
> look for them.  Also, all users will have the same setup, there are
> less degrees of freedom for mistakes, and fluent users can quickly
> pick out what mistakes beginners does, and all scripts work the same
> everywhere.
>
> So, how to work with this setup  in practice?  On Unix-like systems
> this is easy because you can just create so called soft links pointing
> such directories to other places on the file system.  From R and
> aroma.affymetrix, they look the same as regular directories.  This way
> multiple people can share the same data directories.  Unfortunately,
> there is no such feature on MS Windows file system.  However, I added
> support for/follow Windows Shortcut Links, which allow us to emulate
> this.  Thus, you can create a shortcut in the current directory that
> points to the real directory.  You can verify that it works by
> double-clicking on the link in the Windows Explorer and the
> orginal/real directory should open.  I use it all the time on my
> Windows notebook.   This also allows me to keep one working directory
> per project.
>

> C:/Users/pwhiteusa/projectA/, then you want to create the following
> Windows Shortcut links:
>
>   C:/Users/pwhiteusa/projectA/annotationData[.lnk] -> W:/annotationData/
>   C:/Users/pwhiteusa/projectA/rawData[.lnk] -> W:/rawData/
>
> Similarly, you can pre-create output directories to go elsewhere, e.g.
>
>   C:/Users/pwhiteusa/projectA/probeData[.lnk] -> X:/probeData/
>   C:/Users/pwhiteusa/projectA/plmData[.lnk] -> X:/plmData/
>   C:/Users/pwhiteusa/projectA/cbsData[.lnk] -> X:/cbsData/
>   C:/Users/pwhiteusa/projectA/firmaData[.lnk] -> X:/firmaData/
>
> Note that you have to create those directories under X:/.
>
> I write [.lnk], because depending on your setup the filename extension
> *.lnk will be visible or not.  On a default Windows setup they are
> typically not, so then then shortcuts will look like regular
> directories/files.
>
> Also, you can create shortcuts for subdirectories too.  For instance,
> you may have a setup like this:
>
>   C:/Users/pwhiteusa/projectA/annotationData/chipTypes/  # A real directory
>   C:/Users/pwhiteusa/projectA/annotationData/chipTypes/Mapping50K_Hind240/
> # A real directory

>  # A link to

> elsewhere

messages.body_plain:
Hi.

On Tue, Nov 25, 2008 at 10:56 AM, David Rosenberg
<david.m....@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> I apologize if this question has been asked before and I missed it in
> the forums:
>
> How would one go about 'creating' the UFL and UGP files for a cdf/cel
> file collection from scratch?  I have a set of files I am at that were
> left by a previous student without any of this type of information.  I
> believe that there is a way to generate the UFL/UGP (and probably any
> other annotation files) using the NetAffx and/or Fusion SDKs as
> implemented here.  Essentially, the CDF contains only an
> 'uninformative' set of probeset names such as
>
> mm33-3-114836480 (organismBUILD - Chr - pos)
>
> Could someone point me in the right direction?

The UGP and UFL files are handled by the AromaUgpFile and the
AromaUflFile classes which are both subclasses of the
AromaTabularBinaryFile which always defines the underlying binary file
format (see http://groups.google.com/group/aroma-affymetrix/web/aromatabularbinaryfile).

See Page 'Aroma Unit Genome Position (UGP) files'
(http://groups.google.com/group/aroma-affymetrix/web/unit-genome-position-ugp-files)
for examples how to import NetAffx CSV data or other data to UGP files
or manually assign the values.  Note that the records of an UGP file
(and also an UFL file) are indexed by units, that is, each row maps to
the corresponding unit (with the same index) in the CDF.  Since your
unit names (we avoid the term probeset because a unit can contain
multiple groups/sets of probes) have format
<organismBUILD>-<chromosome>-<position> you can infer the (unit,
chromosome, position) from the unit names alone, in case you don't
have an NetAffx CSV file.  For example:

unitNames <- getUnitNames(cdf);
pattern <- "(.*)-(.*)-(.*)";
chr <- gsub(pattern, "\\2", unitNames);
pos <- gsub(pattern, "\\3", unitNames);

chr <- as.integer(chr);  # If there are 'X' and 'Y' you have to deal
with those too.
pos <- as.integer(pos);

Then, allocate an empty UGP file and assign (chr, pos) to it:

ugp <- AromaUgpFile$allocateFromCdf(cdf, tags="mm33,DM20081126");
ugp[,1] <- chr;
ugp[,2] <- pos;

That should do.

You can do similar things for your UFL file.  See Page 'Unit Fragment
Length (UFL) files'
(http://groups.google.com/group/aroma-affymetrix/web/unit-fragment-length-ufl-files)
for further details.

Hope this helps

Henrik

messages.subject: Update on reported issues with generating PNGs using the built-in cairo device
messages.subject_clean: Update on reported issues with generating PNGs using the built-in cairo device
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

previously a few people have reported problems when generating PNGs
using the new built-in cairo device.   From the NEWS file of R v2.8.0
*patched* [http://cran.r-project.org/bin/windows/base/NEWS.R-2.8.0pat]
their is one bug fix that might fix this problem:

BUG FIXES
    ...
    o	bmp(), jpeg(), and png() on unix with type="cairo" would segfault
	on closure if the output file could not be opened.

So, in case you experience segfaults/core dumps when running the
ChromosomeExplorer or ArrayExplorer, try to update to a newer version
of R v2.8.0 *patched*.  If anyone notices that this solves the
problem, please let us know.

Cheers

Henrik

Hi Manasa,

So I get exactly the same results with either of the following:

plm <- RmaPlm(csN, flavor="affyPLM") #according to the documentation
this is the default
plm <- ExonRmaPlm(csN, flavor = "affyPLM", mergeGroups=TRUE) #seems to
take longer to run

However, I noticed that my GeneST normalized data is quite different
from the data that I produce using the Affy package. When looking at
the controls on the array I see that the Aroma normalized data is
between 5-10% lower than that produced by the Bioconductor Affy
packages. However, for some probes this difference is can be quite
large (values are averaged across 16 samples):

Probe                    Bionconductor            Aroma
10341096 (neg_control)   6079                     852
10341735 (neg_control)   25                       87
10340969 (pos_control)   3953                     1758
10338477 (pos_control)   293                      611

Ultimately, when my downstream analysis looks for differential
expression the differences between the two analysis approaches become
minimal, but I did notice that the Aroma package seems to call more
control probes and probes with no known gene as being differentially
expressed (i.e. it looks noisier). These probes were all pretty close
to my 2 fold cutoff, and at 3 fold or greater the data looked the
same.

Do you know where the packages diverge if their probe summation
approach or is it a difference in background correction? I did attempt
to use the flavor="oligo" (as described in the ?RmaPlm help file) but
this returned the following error:

> plm2 <- RmaPlm(csN, flavor="oligo")
> fit(plm2)
Exception: The fit function for requested RMA PLM flavor failed: oligo

Thanks,

Peter

P.S. Here is a summary of the code I used for the Bioconductor
approach:

library(affy)
TestData <- ReadAffy()
TestEset <- rma(TestData)

If you plot(AromaEset[,1],TestEset[,1]) you can visualize how
different the data is.

messages.subject: Re: [aroma.affymetrix] any way to get the name of the SNP as rs#?
messages.subject_clean: [aroma.affymetrix] any way to get the name of the SNP as rs#?
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

On Wed, Nov 26, 2008 at 7:46 AM, mortiz <mort...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> hi everyone,
>
> i was wondering if there is any function which gives as a result the
> names of the SNPs in their "rs#" form?

this mapping information is available in the Affymetrix NetAffx CSV
files, which you can download from the Affymetrix support page for
each chip type.  You find links from the chip type pages on the
aroma.affymetrix site.

An NetAffx CSV file is a large tab-delimited file. Put in under to
corresponding annotationData/ directory and aroma.affymetrix will be
able to find it.  Here is an example how to read such files in
aroma.affymetrix:

The pathname of the NetAffx CSV file is:
annotationData/chipTypes/Mapping250K_Nsp/Affymetrix/Mapping250K_Nsp.na26.annot.csv

library("aroma.affymetrix");
chipType <- "Mapping250K_Nsp";
csv <- AffymetrixNetAffxCsvFile$byChipType(chipType, tags=".na26");
print(csv);

messages.body_plain:
Hi.

a comment on RmaPlm and argument 'flavor':  The RmaPlm class is only
summarizing the probe signals - normalization etc are done before
RmaPlm.   The summarization model is the log-additive model with probe
affinities and chip effects.   The 'flavor' argument specifies which
implementation of the fitting algorithm to use.

The default is "affyPLM", which indicates that it uses the
implementation in 'affyPLM', which now has moved to the
'preprocessCore' package.  Both 'affyPLM' and 'preprocessCore' are
developed and maintained by Ben Bolstad.

The "oligo" flavor was using the fitting algorithm in the 'oligo'
package, which I think in turn originates from the 'affy' package,
which in turn was an early version of Ben Bolstad's code.  I haven't
tried this in awhile, and it appears that 'oligo' has been updated and
the internal function for fitting the model is no longer available.
This is why you get the error message.

Since BB maintain preprocessCore and there has been a lot of
improvements in the algorithm (e.g. it supports probe-specific weights
and much more), I recommend that you use the "affyPLM" flavor.  Since
this is default, you do not have to specify the argument 'flavor' at
all.

For reproducibility of the RMA pipeline in aroma.affymetrix when
compared with 'affyPLM', see Page 'Reproducibility of other
implementations':

  http://groups.google.com/group/aroma-affymetrix/web/redundancy-tests

As you see, the results are remarkable similar.  FYI, for each update
of the package this comparison is part of the redundancy testing.
Note that only PMs are quantile normalized, this might be a reason for
you observing differences.  There is more meat on how
QuantileNormalization and plotDensity() behaves on Page 'Empirical
probe-signal densities and rank-based quantile normalization':

  http://groups.google.com/group/aroma-affymetrix/web/empirical-probe-signal-densities-and-rank-based-quantile-normalization

I am also not sure how similar affyPLM and Affy is, but I trust
affyPLM more than Affy, because I see affyPLM as a more up to date
version of Affy.  Please feel free to contribute with code for
comparing toward Affy.  If you do, please use the same data set.

Cheers

Henrik

> The UGP and UFL files are handled by the AromaUgpFile and the
> AromaUflFile classes which are both subclasses of the
> AromaTabularBinaryFile which always defines the underlying binary file
> format (see http://groups.google.com/group/aroma-affymetrix/web/aromatabularbinaryfile).

> (http://groups.google.com/group/aroma-affymetrix/web/unit-genome-position-ugp-files)

> or manually assign the values.  Note that the records of an UGP file
> (and also an UFL file) are indexed by units, that is, each row maps to
> the corresponding unit (with the same index) in the CDF.  Since your
> unit names (we avoid the term probeset because a unit can contain
> multiple groups/sets of probes) have format
> <organismBUILD>-<chromosome>-<position> you can infer the (unit,
> chromosome, position) from the unit names alone, in case you don't
> have an NetAffx CSV file.  For example:
>
> unitNames <- getUnitNames(cdf);
> pattern <- "(.*)-(.*)-(.*)";
> chr <- gsub(pattern, "\\2", unitNames);
> pos <- gsub(pattern, "\\3", unitNames);
>
> chr <- as.integer(chr);  # If there are 'X' and 'Y' you have to deal
> with those too.
> pos <- as.integer(pos);
>
> Then, allocate an empty UGP file and assign (chr, pos) to it:
>
> ugp <- AromaUgpFile$allocateFromCdf(cdf, tags="mm33,DM20081126");
> ugp[,1] <- chr;
> ugp[,2] <- pos;
>
> That should do.
>
> You can do similar things for your UFL file.  See Page 'Unit Fragment
> Length (UFL) files'
> (http://groups.google.com/group/aroma-affymetrix/web/unit-fragment-length-ufl-files)
> for further details.
>
> Hope this helps

> Henrik

<david.m....@gmail.com> wrote:
> Thank you much for your help.  A couple of follow-ups:
> 1. In terms of 'x', 'y' and 'other' chromosomes (and positions), should I
> just assign 'dummy' values? Should any be left NA?

For the human genome, I map ChrX=23 and ChrY=24.  This seems to be the
de facto standard.   For mitochondrial DNA, I've assigned it ChrM=25.
I don't know of a standard for this.

It is ok to have NAs, that is, for those units you cannot map
estimates to the genome.  They will not show up in the
ChromosomeExplorer and they will not be part of any segmentation
either and so.

> 2. Lacking a NetAffx csv file, how might I determine fragment lengths?

I have no aces for this.  If you know the restriction enzymes used,
you can find out at what locations they digest the DNA.  This
information will define the lengths of all digested fragments.  Then
you have to map the units in your CDF to these fragments.   I haven't
done this myself and you will have to turn to external resources for
identifying the locations etc.

You could also try to contact Affymetrix to see if they have this
information for your custom CDF.

Cheers

/Henrik

Hi all.

Just to follow up on these comments here.

'fitPLM' with default parameters in the affyPLM package should give
practically identical results to the 'standard' pipeline (RMA bg corr
+ quantile + fit) within aroma.affymetrix, assuming the underlying
annotation is the same.  This was an easy comparison back in the day
of 3' IVT arrays.  Now, its a little more difficult.

If anyone is willing, I'd be keen to know if these two actually do
give the same results on the newer chips i.e. is the underlying
annotation the same?  I seem to recall that because these newer chips
occasionally have probes that are shared amongst different probesets,
that the older style affy package would not be able to handle it.  For
example, Jim MacDonald's post:

http://article.gmane.org/gmane.science.biology.informatics.conductor/19184

Jim says there that you "don't want to use affy" for these chips (not
100% sure why).  He suggests the whole pdInfoBuilder/oligo thing which
at one time had some bugs, but is probably more stable now.  I haven't
dug deeper as to whether the annotation that 'fitPLM' uses by default
('hugene10st.db' presumably?) matches the annotation that would be
used by aroma.affymetrix (the converted-to-binary 'unsupported' CDF
file).  I know Mark Cowley did find some inconsistencies:

http://article.gmane.org/gmane.science.biology.informatics.conductor/19738

This makes me think that we may want to alternatively construct the
XXGene 1.0 CDFs (XX=Hu,Mo,Ra) directly from the PGF/CLF files instead
of from the unsupported CDF.  I suspect that there will only be minor
changes, so I haven't looked too deeply into it.

Anyone want to check?

In addition to what Henrik says about flavour="affyPLM" ... for a lot
of my work, there is definitely additional value in using the
auxiliary information from the PLMs (i.e. weights, residuals) ... you
don't get this directly with oligo/median polish.

Few more specific notes ...

>> library(affy)
>> TestData <- ReadAffy()
>> TestEset <- rma(TestData)
>>
>> If you plot(AromaEset[,1],TestEset[,1]) you can visualize how
>> different the data is.

I assume you ensured the probesets and samples are in the same order?
(Or, is this somehow covered by the plot method ...)  I can't tell
from this sequence of commands.  I don't know what this plot looks
like, so I don't whether to be alarmed or not.

>> However, I noticed that my GeneST normalized data is quite different
>> from the data that I produce using the Affy package. When looking at
>> the controls on the array I see that the Aroma normalized data is
>> between 5-10% lower than that produced by the Bioconductor Affy
>> packages. However, for some probes this difference is can be quite
>> large (values are averaged across 16 samples):
>>
>> Probe                    Bionconductor            Aroma
>> 10341096 (neg_control)   6079                     852
>> 10341735 (neg_control)   25                       87
>> 10340969 (pos_control)   3953                     1758
>> 10338477 (pos_control)   293                      611
>>
>> Ultimately, when my downstream analysis looks for differential
>> expression the differences between the two analysis approaches become
>> minimal, but I did notice that the Aroma package seems to call more
>> control probes and probes with no known gene as being differentially
>> expressed (i.e. it looks noisier). These probes were all pretty close
>> to my 2 fold cutoff, and at 3 fold or greater the data looked the
>> same.

Tough to really tell.  You'd probably want to average on the log2
scale, not the linear scale.  This could be a difference in median-
polish versus robust PLM, or could be a differnce in annotation.
Requires some digging.

Also, you may want to remove control probesets before doing DE
analysis --- for one thing, you pay a slightly lesser penalty for
multiple testing.

Cheers,
Mark

messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I am seeing a strange artefact in my SNP6.0 data when processed by
writeImage function.

>lapply(cs.Plate6, writeImage, tags="rainbow", palette=rainbow(256))

It looks like a small square with diagonal red stripes and looks far
too regular to be generated artificially. It occurs on more than one
chip in the experiment but not always in the same place.  I got in
touch with the people running the arrays and they do not see it
through Affymetrix software. So I wonder if this is a problem caused
by aroma.

I can send an example file to illustrate the problem.

Thanks,

Mark

Please do.  Do *not* rescale it etc, because if you do, then you can
get funny artifacts that are not true.  Make sure to post your
complete script as well (even if it is an obvious one).  If you have
some extra information on the data, that'll be good too.

I don't think the Affymetrix can display arrays in a rainbow map,
which could be why they don't see it there.  Can you see it if you use
a, say, "yellow" color map.  There is probably a simple explanation.
It doubt that there is a bug in aroma.affymetrix generating this, but
you never know.
